summary: Extends the SIP registration event package, from RFC 3680, so watchers can learn the GRUUs of registered devices. Registered contacts are often unreachable by others, so a GRUU is more useful.

eli5.summary: A phone book entry that nobody can dial is not helpful. This lets the phone book list the dialable number for each device.

questions: what is a gruu in sip
subtitle: Two small XML elements that let SIP registration notifications carry a device's globally reachable address.

tldr.problem: The SIP registration event package reports a device's registered contact, but that address is often private or behind a firewall, so watchers cannot use it. The GRUUs the registrar assigned were not reported at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines pub-gruu and temp-gruu elements that go inside the contact element of a registration notification. The temp-gruu element also carries a first-cseq attribute that tells a device which temporary GRUUs are still valid.
tldr.outcome: Watchers and the devices themselves can learn every GRUU, including those of implicitly registered addresses of record. The RFC recommends handing temporary GRUUs only to subscribers who are allowed to register to the address of record.

today: RFC 5628 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3680 and RFC 5627.

sections.title: Why Registered Contacts Are Not Enough
sections.content:
RFC 3680 defines a SIP event package that lets a watcher learn what a registrar stores, including the registered contacts. The trouble is that a registered contact is frequently unreachable from hosts outside the user agent's domain. It is commonly a private address, or a public one that firewalls block.

A GRUU (Globally Routable User Agent URI, from RFC 5627) reaches one particular user agent instance and can be used from anywhere on the Internet. But GRUUs assigned by the registrar were not part of RFC 3680 notifications, even though many applications need the GRUU and not the contact.

Two examples drive the design. The Welcome Notices example in RFC 3680 only works if the sender can reach the contact, so it should send its MESSAGE to a GRUU. And in the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), one REGISTER can implicitly register the same contact to other associated addresses of record, each needing its own GRUUs that are hard to tell the device about.
sections.eli5: A phone number that only works inside your house is no use to friends outside. This makes the phone book show the number that works from anywhere.

sections.title: The Two New Elements
sections.content:
The registration event package lets extension elements sit inside the <contact> element. This RFC uses that room to define two optional elements, <pub-gruu> and <temp-gruu>, each holding a GRUU. The <temp-gruu> element also identifies the oldest temporary GRUU that is currently valid.

They appear in the body of a NOTIFY when GRUUs are associated with the contact, so the contact URI and the GRUUs are all available to the watcher. Handling of SUBSCRIBE requests is unchanged from RFC 3680.

The elements live in a new XML namespace, urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:gruuinfo. In the schema, pub-gruu has a required uri attribute, and temp-gruu extends it with a required first-cseq attribute of type unsigned long.
sections.eli5: Each device's phone book entry gets two extra lines: a long-lasting number and a throwaway number that can be changed.

sections.title: What Notifiers and Subscribers Do
sections.content:
A notifier SHOULD include <pub-gruu> when a contact has an instance ID and a public GRUU exists for that AOR and instance ID. It MAY include <temp-gruu> when a temporary GRUU exists. The temporary one SHOULD be included if the subscriber is also authorized to register to the AOR, and SHOULD NOT be included otherwise, unless an explicitly configured policy says to. Either element MUST be a child of <contact>.

The public GRUU element MUST hold the public GRUU for the instance ID and AOR. The temporary one MUST hold the most recently assigned temporary GRUU, and MUST carry a first-cseq value: the CSeq of the REGISTER request that caused the oldest currently active temporary GRUU to be assigned.

Several contacts can share one instance ID, so their elements will be identical. A contact has only one instance ID, so it never has more than one of each element.

A subscriber MAY associate a received public GRUU with the AOR and instance ID, and MUST discard any earlier public GRUU for the same pair, because it no longer works. It MAY likewise keep a temporary GRUU along with its callid and cseq. Subscribers unaware of the extension ignore the new elements, as RFC 3680 requires.
sections.eli5: The phone book keeper puts both numbers on the entry. Anyone who reads it keeps the newest long-lasting number and throws away the old one.

sections.title: Keeping Only Valid Temporary GRUUs
sections.content:
Under RFC 5627, temporary GRUUs stop working when bindings are not refreshed or when a registration is made with a new Call-ID. A user agent cannot always tell which ones are still valid from REGISTER responses or plain RFC 3680 notifications. This extension supplies the missing information.

The RFC lists steps a UA MAY take. It should subscribe to the registration event for the AOR it registers. On a 2xx response to REGISTER it may keep the temporary GRUU, noting the Call-ID and CSeq of that response. When a notification arrives with a <temp-gruu> for its contact and instance ID, it may add that GRUU and should remove any saved GRUU whose callid differs, or whose cseq is less than the first-cseq value.

If a notification for a supported AOR has no <contact> entries for the UA's instance ID, the UA should discard all temporary GRUUs it saved for that AOR.
sections.eli5: It is like checking a list of spare keys. The notice says which keys still open the door, so you throw away the ones that no longer fit.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Section 7 gives a sample reginfo document where a contact has both <gr:pub-gruu> and <gr:temp-gruu> (with first-cseq="54301"). In the Welcome Notice example, the application server sees that notification and addresses its MESSAGE to the public GRUU, not the unreachable contact.

The IMS example shows a UA sending one REGISTER that asks for GRUUs. The 200 response returns GRUUs only for the AOR explicitly registered, and names two other associated AORs in a P-Associated-URI header. The UA then sends a SUBSCRIBE with Event: reg, and the first NOTIFY lists all three AORs, each with its own unique pub-gruu and temp-gruu. The UA can keep those GRUUs for dialogs using the corresponding AORs.
sections.eli5: One phone signs up and the phone book then lists three names for it, each with its own working number.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 3680 apply. Disclosing a GRUU adds little risk: requests to a GRUU are first processed by the servicing proxy, which can control access just as it can for the AOR, for example with a white list.

Temporary GRUUs are different, because they are meant to be a contact address that cannot be correlated with the caller's identity. Someone could guess the caller and try to fetch its temporary GRUUs by sending REGISTER or a registration SUBSCRIBE. The RFC recommends that only subscribers authorized to register to the AOR receive temporary GRUUs. It also warns that confidentiality does not extend to parties permitted to register to the AOR.

For IANA, the RFC registers the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:gruuinfo and the schema urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:gruuinfo.
sections.eli5: Showing a number that goes through a doorman is fairly safe. The throwaway number is only shown to people who are already allowed to use the house.

viz.caption: CONTACT ELEMENT WITH GRUUS (ADAPTED FROM RFC 5628 SECTION 7)

data.title: Contact with GRUU elements
data.code:
<contact id="76" state="active" event="registered"
    callid="1j9FpLxk3uxtm8tn@192.0.2.1" cseq="54321">
  <uri>sip:user@192.0.2.1</uri>
  <gr:pub-gruu uri="sip:user@example.com;gr=hha9s8d-999a"/>
  <gr:temp-gruu uri="sip:8ffkas08af7fasklzi9@example.com;gr"
      first-cseq="54301"/>
</contact>
